planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; check local invasive species listings before planting near natural woodland areas, since the species can escape cultivation in parts of the eastern US.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; more compact and better-behaved as a mounding shrub than as an aggressive climber compared to the plain species. Emerald Gaiety is a longtime favorite variegated euonymus cultivar, its glossy, oval, dark-green leaves crisply edged in white, turning a soft pink-tinged blush in cold winter weather for added seasonal interest. It grows as a low, mounding shrub when unsupported or will climb given a wall or trellis to attach to, making it flexible as a foundation shrub, low hedge, or wall cover. It is tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, poor soil, and air pollution, but is susceptible to euonymus scale, so monitor closely and treat promptly if scale insects appear.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; brightest gold variegation develops with a few hours of direct sun. Emerald 'n Gold is a compact, colorful euonymus cultivar with glossy green leaves broadly edged in bright golden-yellow, taking on a pink-red blush through winter cold that adds a second color phase beyond the summer gold-and-green look. Like other euonymus fortunei cultivars, it grows as a low, spreading mound if unsupported or climbs given a wall or trellis, making it a versatile, bright accent for foundation plantings, low borders, or trained against a fence. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and air pollution well, but watch for euonymus scale and treat promptly if it appears.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container vines near a very sturdy support structure in spring; like the species, Flava is vigorous, heavy, and spreads by root suckers, so control spread promptly by mowing or digging out suckers.

directions: Plant near a very sturdy fence, masonry wall, pergola, or large tree in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil. Flava is a yellow-flowered selection of the native trumpet vine, replacing the species' typical orange-red trumpet flowers with clear, bright golden-yellow blooms from June through September, while retaining the same vigorous, aerial-root climbing habit and importance as hummingbird forage. Like the straight species, it is extremely vigorous, spreading by root suckers and capable of quickly covering — or overwhelming — a support structure, so it needs a genuinely sturdy structure and regular control of suckers around the base. The sap can cause skin irritation in some people; wear gloves when pruning or handling the vine.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring near a trellis, fence, or other support; stems twine and will climb 10–15 feet.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle, this native selection is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. Dropmore Scarlet is a hybrid honeysuckle noted for its exceptionally long bloom season, producing clusters of long, tubular, bright scarlet-red flowers continuously from late spring through frost rather than the more sporadic rebloom typical of straight coral honeysuckle, making it one of the most reliable season-long hummingbird plants available. Prune in late winter or right after a bloom flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood. It is semi-evergreen in mild climates, holding foliage through many winters in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; well-behaved and non-invasive, unlike Japanese honeysuckle. John Clayton is a yellow-flowered selection of native coral honeysuckle, discovered in Virginia and named for the 18th-century botanist, bearing long, tubular, clear yellow flowers instead of the species' typical scarlet-to-coral color, with a long bloom season from spring through fall and light rebloom. It provides the same long-tube nectar source ruby-throated hummingbirds rely on, while giving gardeners a color alternative to the more common red-flowered selections for pairing with other warm-toned plantings. Prune in late winter or just after a bloom flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood; semi-evergreen in mild Gulf South winters.

common_name: Joan J Raspberry (Thornless Primocane Everbearing Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Joan J fruits on primocanes (first-year canes), so it can be mown to the ground each winter for simplified maintenance.

directions: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring, and mow or cut all canes to the ground each winter for the simplest maintenance approach, since Joan J bears fruit on the current year's primocanes rather than needing overwintered floricanes. This thornless, everbearing raspberry produces a large early-summer crop plus a second flush in fall, with smooth, spine-free canes that make picking and pruning far more pleasant than thorny raspberry cultivars. It is notably vigorous and disease-resistant, producing large, firm, richly flavored berries over an extended harvest window. Support canes with a simple two-wire trellis if grown for the full season rather than mown annually, and harvest when berries pull cleanly from the plug with no resistance.
